scenes.narration: What is F S L? Meet the collection of tools used to inspect, preprocess, model, and report M R I data. The goal is clear: Describe F S L as a suite rather than one application.

display.title: FSL is a toolkit, not a single program
display.body: FSL—the FMRIB Software Library—is a collection of command-line tools and graphical interfaces for MRI analysis. FEAT handles fMRI modeling, FSLEyes displays images, and utilities such as fslinfo, fslstats, and fslmaths inspect or transform data.

scenes.narration: F S L is a toolkit, not a single program. F S L—the F M R I B Software Library—is a collection of command-line tools and graphical interfaces for M R I analysis. FEAT handles functional M R I modeling, F S L Eyes displays images, and utilities such as F S L info, F S L stats, and F S L maths inspect or transform data. A typical workflow moves between tools. You might inspect a raw bold image in F S L Eyes, configure a model in FEAT, run it, then return to F S L Eyes to check registration and statistical maps. Learning F S L therefore means learning both the scientific purpose of each step and the output it produces.

display.title: A reproducible software environment
display.body: Neurodesk packages neuroimaging applications in consistent environments. Neurodesk Play is broadly accessible; Neurodesk EDU may be provided by a course or institution; a local installation is optional and has higher hardware requirements.
display.imageCaption: The local launcher shown in the source lab. Browser-based Play and EDU sessions have a similar app workspace.

scenes.narration: A reproducible software environment. Neurodesk packages neuroimaging applications in consistent environments. Neurodesk Play is broadly accessible; Neurodesk EDU may be provided by a course or institution; a local installation is optional and has higher hardware requirements. Files saved only inside temporary browser sessions may disappear. Use the persistent storage location provided by your environment. The base terminal is useful for general Linux work; an F S L terminal starts with the F S L software environment already loaded.

display.title: Your working directory is context

scenes.narration: What is a NIfTI image? Interpret the dimensions and spatial metadata stored in .nii and .nii.gz files. The goal is clear: Differentiate voxels and volumes.

display.title: A 4D image is a time-ordered stack of 3D volumes
display.body: A voxel is a three-dimensional sample. An anatomical NIfTI is usually one 3D volume; a BOLD NIfTI usually contains many volumes along a fourth, temporal dimension. Header metadata records dimensions, voxel sizes, orientation, and timing.

scenes.narration: A four-D image is a time-ordered stack of three-D volumes. A voxel is a three-dimensional sample. An anatomical NIfTI is usually one three-D volume; a bold NIfTI usually contains many volumes along a fourth, temporal dimension. Header metadata records dimensions, voxel sizes, orientation, and timing. If dim4 is 240, the bold series contains 240 volumes. Spatial resolution comes from pixdim1 through pixdim3; pixdim4 often records the T R in seconds. Always verify the units in the header and JSON sidecar.

display.title: Structure is part of the data
display.body: The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) uses predictable folders and filenames so people and software can identify participants, sessions, tasks, runs, and modalities without relying on local naming conventions.

scenes.narration: Structure is part of the data. The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) uses predictable folders and filenames so people and software can identify participants, sessions, tasks, runs, and modalities without relying on local naming conventions. A functional run lives under sub-*/func/ and pairs a _bold.nii.gz image with a _bold.json sidecar. Its _events.tsv file describes event onsets and durations. Anatomical T1-weighted data typically live under sub-*/anat/.

display.title: One coordinate, several sources of evidence
display.body: Overlays let you compare images in the same coordinate space. Time-series plots show how a voxel changes across volumes. Atlas lookup adds an anatomical label, but atlas boundaries are probabilistic and should not be treated as ground truth for every participant.

scenes.narration: One coordinate, several sources of evidence. Overlays let you compare images in the same coordinate space. Time-series plots show how a voxel changes across volumes. Atlas lookup adds an anatomical label, but atlas boundaries are probabilistic and should not be treated as ground truth for every participant. Registration quality control is easiest when boundaries from two images can be seen together. Alternate visibility, adjust opacity, or use an edge overlay. For functional data, look for sudden spikes, drifts, or dropout and relate them to later motion and preprocessing reports.

scenes.narration: F S L info and F S L stats. Inspect image metadata and compute targeted summary statistics. The goal is clear: Choose F S L info for metadata.

display.title: Metadata describes the container; statistics describe its values
display.body: `fslinfo` reports header fields such as dimensions and voxel sizes. `fslstats` computes statistics over image intensities, optionally after applying thresholds or masks. A number is only interpretable when you know which voxels contributed to it.

scenes.narration: Metadata describes the container; statistics describe its values. F S L info reports header fields such as dimensions and voxel sizes. F S L stats computes statistics over image intensities, optionally after applying thresholds or masks. A number is only interpretable when you know which voxels contributed to it. For example, F S L stats image -R reports the robust intensity range. -V reports the number and physical volume of nonzero voxels. Nonzero voxels are not automatically the brain; background noise, skull, or artifacts may also be nonzero.

display.title: What is a GLM?
display.body: The general linear model represents the measured BOLD time series as a weighted combination of explanatory variables plus unexplained residual error. FEAT fits this model separately at each voxel while accounting for temporal structure.

scenes.narration: What is a G L M? The general linear model represents the measured bold time series as a weighted combination of explanatory variables plus unexplained residual error. FEAT fits this model separately at each voxel while accounting for temporal structure. The design matrix contains one row per time point and columns for task predictors and nuisance regressors. Parameter estimates describe each column's contribution. A good-looking activation map cannot rescue a design matrix that does not represent the experiment.

display.title: What is an explanatory variable?
display.body: An explanatory variable (EV) represents a pattern expected to explain some variation in the data. Task events, parametric values, motion estimates, and other confounds can all become EVs, but their interpretations differ.

scenes.narration: What is an explanatory variable? An explanatory variable (E V) represents a pattern expected to explain some variation in the data. Task events, parametric values, motion estimates, and other confounds can all become E V's, but their interpretations differ. FEAT begins with the event timing you specify, convolves task E V's with a hemodynamic response, and may add temporal derivatives. Each resulting column consumes model degrees of freedom, so include predictors for a reason—not simply because they are available.

display.title: The HRF and convolution
display.body: The hemodynamic response function (HRF) approximates the delayed, smooth BOLD response that follows brief neural activity. Convolution combines event timing with this response shape to create a model predictor.

scenes.narration: The H R F and convolution. The hemodynamic response function (H R F) approximates the delayed, smooth bold response that follows brief neural activity. Convolution combines event timing with this response shape to create a model predictor. The predictor should resemble the signal you expect to measure, not an instantaneous event list. FEAT offers basis choices and temporal derivatives, but extra flexibility changes the model and interpretation. Use the course or study protocol rather than defaulting blindly.

videos.title: Reviewing a complete FEAT report
videos.description: Review a completed FEAT report as an ordered chain of quality-control evidence.

display.title: Reviewing a complete FEAT report
display.body: Treat the report as a chain of evidence, not a gallery of activation maps.

scenes.narration: A completed FEAT report is not automatically a valid analysis. It is a structured record that lets you review preprocessing, registration, model design, and statistical output in an evidence-based order. This video shows how to read that record before interpreting bright clusters or reporting a result.

display.title: Inputs before inference
display.body: Later results depend on every earlier stage.
bullets: Pre-stats: motion and preprocessing
Registration: anatomical correspondence
Stats: design matrix and contrasts
Post-stats: thresholded inference
display.imageCaption: Real FEAT report captured in the adapted source curriculum.

scenes.narration: Review the report in dependency order. Begin with Pre-stats and ask whether motion, masking, and preprocessing outputs are plausible. Continue to Registration and inspect alignment across the brain. Then examine the design matrix, explanatory variables, and contrasts under Stats. Only after those checks should you interpret thresholded results under Post-stats. A failure early in this chain limits what later pages can support.

display.title: What did you actually check?
bullets: Motion: acceptable, concerning, or unusable—and why?
Registration: where do boundaries agree or fail?
Design: do timing, columns, and contrasts match the protocol?
display.imageCaption: Registration evidence from the source workflow.

scenes.narration: Write one defensible statement for each major dependency. For motion, describe the plot and any abrupt displacement rather than saying it looks fine. For registration, name anatomical boundaries and multiple slices that support a pass or concern. For the design, match columns to timing files and contrast arrows to the planned hypothesis. Specific observations are auditable; vague reassurance is not.

display.title: A z-statistic is not an effect size
display.body: Interpret cope, uncertainty, standardized evidence, and thresholded display as related but different outputs.
bullets: cope: estimated contrast effect
varcope: uncertainty
t or z: standardized evidence
thresholded map: inferential display

scenes.narration: When you reach the results, keep the output types separate. A cope is the estimated contrast effect. A varcope describes uncertainty in that estimate. A t-statistic or z-statistic standardizes evidence relative to uncertainty. A thresholded map displays locations surviving the chosen inferential procedure. Do not describe a z-statistic map as an effect-size map, and do not let an attractive cluster override failed motion, registration, or design checks.

display.title: Pass, concern, or fail—with evidence
display.body: A complete analysis includes a written QC judgment, not only a dot feat directory.
bullets: Name the evidence reviewed
Record concerns and their likely impact
Link conclusions to the approved analysis plan
Preserve the report and design

scenes.narration: Finish with an explicit quality-control decision: pass, concern, or fail, followed by the evidence that supports it. Record any limitation and explain how it affects interpretation. Preserve the report, design files, and notes together. The purpose of review is not to prove that FEAT completed. It is to decide whether this run can support the scientific claim you intend to make.
